title: Critical Thinking: Foundations
description: A six-chapter guided course on disciplined reasoning, thinking traps, the eight-step process, tool selection, Project Relay, and personal transfer.
author: Joshua Mayne

blocks.title: Better thinking begins before better decisions.

blocks.body: Every day, we interpret information, make assumptions, solve problems, and make decisions. The question isn't whether you think. The question is how well you examine your thinking before acting on it.
Your team has missed the same performance target for three consecutive months.
Several employees say the problem is inadequate training. A supervisor agrees and recommends mandatory refresher training.

blocks.title: What should happen next?

options.text: B. Determine why employees aren't applying their training.
C. Gather additional evidence before defining the problem.
options.feedback: There isn't enough information yet. The pressure to solve a problem often arrives before we've adequately defined it. Critical thinking helps us resist that pressure.

options.text: D. Ask management what solution they prefer.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: There isn't enough information yet. The pressure to solve a problem often arrives before we've adequately defined it. Critical thinking helps us resist that pressure.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Review the explanation and compare each option with the evidence. There isn't enough information yet. The pressure to solve a problem often arrives before we've adequately defined it. Critical thinking helps us resist that pressure.

blocks.body: Before improving your thinking, understand what critical thinking actually is.

blocks.title: Disciplined thinking used to improve the quality of our judgments and decisions.

blocks.body: It requires us to deliberately examine:

• What do I know?
  • How do I know it?
  • What am I assuming?
  • What else could explain this?
  • Does the evidence support my conclusion?
Critical thinking isn't about thinking more. It's about thinking better.
Open each concept. All four must be explored before you continue.

items.back: Thinking deliberately rather than simply reacting.
Distinguishing what is known from what is believed or assumed.
Testing explanations, assumptions, and your own reasoning.
Thinking toward an informed judgment, decision, or action.

blocks.title: Good reasoning is often confused with other behaviors.

blocks.body: Open all six cards to reveal the distinction.

items.back: Finding fault isn't the same as examining reasoning.
Winning an argument doesn't necessarily mean reaching a sound conclusion.
More analysis doesn't automatically produce better analysis.
Experience can provide useful signals; it simply shouldn't escape examination.
A tool can structure thinking. It cannot think for you.
Expertise helps, but expertise can also create assumptions and blind spots.

Next: why capable people still fall into predictable thinking traps.
Good people can make poor decisions for perfectly understandable reasons.

blocks.title: Thinking shortcuts are useful—until they aren't.

blocks.body: Human thinking relies on shortcuts. That's usually useful. We recognize patterns, draw on experience, and make thousands of judgments without consciously analyzing each one.
But efficiency has a cost. Under pressure, uncertainty, emotion, or familiarity, a useful shortcut can become a thinking trap.
Critical thinkers don't eliminate these tendencies. They learn to notice them.
Open each one. The goal is not memorizing labels—it is recognizing what the trap looks like in your own reasoning.

items.back: We favor information that supports what we already believe and discount evidence that challenges it.
Early information becomes a reference point and can influence later judgment more than it deserves.
Recent, vivid, or memorable information feels more important or more common than it may actually be.
The desire for agreement or cohesion suppresses questions, alternatives, and constructive disagreement.
We stop searching once we find an explanation that seems good enough—even when important questions remain.
Our confidence in a conclusion exceeds the quality or completeness of the evidence supporting it.

blocks.title: Thinking trap 1
blocks.body: An experienced manager recognizes a familiar pattern and immediately favors the explanation that worked last time. New data points in another direction, but she dismisses it as an exception.

options.feedback: Confirmation bias. Experience created an initial explanation, and contradictory evidence was discounted rather than examined.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Confirmation bias. Experience created an initial explanation, and contradictory evidence was discounted rather than examined.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Review the explanation and compare each option with the evidence. Confirmation bias. Experience created an initial explanation, and contradictory evidence was discounted rather than examined.

blocks.title: Thinking trap 2
blocks.body: The first estimate discussed in a planning meeting is $250,000. Every later estimate is debated mainly in relation to that original number, even though no one knows how it was calculated.

options.feedback: Anchoring. The first number became the reference point before its quality was established.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Anchoring. The first number became the reference point before its quality was established.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Review the explanation and compare each option with the evidence. Anchoring. The first number became the reference point before its quality was established.

blocks.title: Thinking trap 3
blocks.body: After two highly visible incidents this month, a team concludes the problem is rapidly increasing, even though the annual data shows no meaningful change.

options.feedback: Availability. Recent, vivid events are receiving more weight than the broader evidence.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Availability. Recent, vivid events are receiving more weight than the broader evidence.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Review the explanation and compare each option with the evidence. Availability. Recent, vivid events are receiving more weight than the broader evidence.

blocks.body: A team quickly agrees on a solution proposed by its respected leader. Several members have concerns but decide raising them would only slow the meeting down.

options.feedback: Groupthink. The pressure for cohesion is suppressing constructive challenge.

blocks.title: Not every barrier has a psychological label.

blocks.body: The environment around us can make disciplined thinking harder. Open each factor.

items.back: Urgency can push us toward the first workable explanation rather than the best-supported one.
Strong emotion can narrow attention and change which evidence feels important.
Rank or expertise can discourage people from testing assumptions or voicing contradictory evidence.
Social costs can make agreement easier than constructive challenge.
More information is not always better; volume can hide relevance and weaken prioritization.
Experience accelerates pattern recognition, but familiar patterns can cause us to overlook what is different this time.

blocks.body: A disciplined path from uncertainty to defensible judgment.

blocks.title: Structure your thinking without turning it into a rigid formula.

blocks.body: Critical thinking is iterative. New information may send you backward. A question may change how you define the problem. Analysis may reveal an unknown that requires more evidence.

items.title: DEFINE
items.text: Clarify the actual problem before attempting to solve it.

items.title: UNDERSTAND
items.text: Separate what is known from what is inferred and what is still unknown.

items.title: QUESTION
items.text: Test the situation and your own reasoning with deliberate questions.

items.title: ANALYZE
items.text: Break the situation apart, then reconnect the pieces to understand meaning.

items.title: EXPLORE
items.text: Generate multiple explanations and possibilities before committing.

items.title: EVALUATE
items.text: Use criteria and evidence to compare alternatives and tradeoffs.

items.title: DECIDE
items.text: Make a defensible judgment and communicate how it was reached.

items.title: REFLECT
items.text: Examine the result and your own reasoning so the next decision improves.

blocks.title: Not every complex problem has one root cause.

blocks.body: Searching for the root cause can encourage premature certainty when outcomes are actually produced by several interacting conditions.
A stronger question is often: “What combination of conditions could be producing this outcome?”
You have built the front half of the reasoning process.
Strong judgment requires alternatives, criteria, evidence, and an honest look at tradeoffs.
Our first reasonable idea often gains an unfair advantage simply because it arrived first.
Delay commitment long enough to create alternatives.

blocks.body: A tool can organize your reasoning. It cannot replace it.

blocks.title: Choose the tool that serves the thinking—not the other way around.

blocks.body: Move horizontally through the toolkit. Select a card to see when the tool helps, what it produces, and when it can mislead you.

blocks.title: When, why, and how to use each tool

items.title: 5 Whys
items.text:
When: When a relatively straightforward problem may have a causal chain worth probing.

How it helps: Pushes beyond the first explanation by repeatedly asking what produced the condition.

Watch for: Do not force five levels or assume a complex system has one linear root cause.

items.title: Stakeholder Map
items.text:
When: When different people or groups influence, experience, or are affected by a decision.

How it helps: Makes interests, influence, impact, missing voices, and potential resistance visible.

Watch for: Do not treat stakeholder assumptions as facts. Validate important perspectives directly.

items.title: Mind Map
items.text:
When: When the issue is broad, messy, or still being explored.

How it helps: Externalizes ideas and relationships so patterns, categories, and missing areas become easier to see.

Watch for: Do not mistake a crowded map for analysis. Connections still require evidence and interpretation.

items.title: SWOT
items.text:
When: When you need a high-level scan of internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.

How it helps: Creates a shared strategic snapshot and prompts both internal and external examination.

Watch for: Do not use vague labels or stop at four lists. The value comes from evidence and implications.

items.title: Assumption Testing
items.text:
When: When a recommendation depends on beliefs that may not have been verified.

How it helps: Surfaces assumptions, rates their importance and uncertainty, and identifies what should be tested first.

Watch for: Do not test only assumptions you already doubt. High-impact assumptions supporting your preferred answer matter most.

items.title: Evidence Matrix
items.text:
When: When several claims or explanations compete and the evidence is mixed.

How it helps: Compares what supports, contradicts, or is missing for each claim.

Watch for: Do not count pieces of evidence as if all evidence has equal quality, relevance, or independence.

items.title: Decision Matrix
items.text:
When: When multiple viable options must be compared against explicit criteria.

How it helps: Makes criteria, weighting, tradeoffs, and comparisons visible and discussable.

Watch for: Do not let scores create false precision. Weak criteria and weak evidence still produce weak decisions.

items.title: Tradeoff Analysis
items.text:
When: When every realistic option has meaningful benefits, costs, risks, or opportunity costs.

How it helps: Forces an explicit look at what is gained, what is sacrificed, and who bears the consequences.

Watch for: Do not reduce important qualitative consequences to a simple pros-and-cons count.

blocks.title: Good tool use begins before you open the template.

blocks.body: You need structure for a specific reasoning task: finding relationships, testing assumptions, comparing alternatives, organizing evidence, or seeing stakeholders.

blocks.title: Do not use a tool just because…

blocks.body: It is familiar, impressive, required by habit, or available. A polished framework can create false confidence if it is answering the wrong question.
The simplest adequate method is often the strongest. Sometimes the right “tool” is a better question or one missing piece of evidence.

blocks.body: Next: apply the complete critical-thinking process to one realistic organizational challenge.

blocks.title: YOU KNOW THE LANGUAGE. NOW THINK.

blocks.body: One organizational challenge. Eight stages. Your reasoning determines what happens next.
A service unit that coordinates time-sensitive requests has missed its 24-hour processing target for ten consecutive weeks.
Leadership's initial proposal: mandatory refresher training for all employees.
Your job is not to defend or reject that proposal. Your job is to determine what the evidence supports.

blocks.title: What you know at the start.

blocks.body:
Performance: On-time processing fell from 91% to 73% over ten weeks.
Workload: Incoming volume increased 8% during the same period.
Change: A new intake-and-routing procedure began eleven weeks ago.
Training: 94% of employees completed required procedure training before launch.
Employee reports: Several employees describe conflicting guidance about priority cases.
Unknown: No one has compared delays by shift, case type, routing path, or supervisor.
Resist the urge to solve the case now. Your information will expand as your questions improve.

blocks.title: You do not need to remember every screen. Remember these.

blocks.body: Select each card and move horizontally through the principles.

items.back: Describe the gap before you attach a cause or remedy. A neutral problem statement protects the inquiry from premature closure.
Facts, interpretations, and unknowns can all be useful—but only when you know which is which.
Do not only interrogate the problem. Ask what you are assuming, what contradicts your view, and what would change your mind.
Create alternatives before selecting among them. The first reasonable idea should not automatically become the answer.
Confidence should rise or fall with the quality of the evidence. Revising confidence is disciplined reasoning, not indecision.

blocks.title: Turn insight into a behavior you can use.

blocks.body: What should tell you that you may be moving too quickly or becoming too certain?

blocks.title: My warning sign
blocks.body: I should slow down when…
Choose one question you can use to interrupt automatic thinking.

blocks.title: My reset question
blocks.body: Before I decide, I will ask…

blocks.title: What happens next is intentionally harder.

blocks.body: This course gave you the language and foundation. The live classroom is where you will use it under ambiguity, competing perspectives, incomplete information, and time pressure.
Expect to explain what you believe, why you believe it, and what would change your mind.
Expect facts, inferences, unknowns, and contradictory information to arrive together.
Expect to make a recommendation and make the path to that recommendation visible.
Your goal in class is not to be the fastest person to an answer. It is to improve the quality of the reasoning that produces the answer.

blocks.title: Five decisions. One last look at the fundamentals.

questions.title: Before proposing a solution, the strongest first move is to…

options.text: Identify the performance gap without assuming its cause.
options.feedback: The strongest answer is: Identify the performance gap without assuming its cause.

options.text: Choose the most familiar analytical tool.
Ask the most experienced person for the answer.

questions.title: Which statement best reflects disciplined evidence use?

options.text: A plausible inference can be treated as a fact when time is short.
Confidence should match the quality and completeness of the evidence.
options.feedback: The strongest answer is: Confidence should match the quality and completeness of the evidence.

options.text: More information always produces a better decision.

options.text: Before converging on a preferred solution.

options.text: Use the most comprehensive tool available.
Use a tool because the template creates objectivity.
Choose a tool only when it serves a specific reasoning need.

options.text: Whether other people agreed with the decision.
The outcome and the quality of the reasoning that produced it.

blocks.body: You know the foundation. Now come prepared to challenge assumptions, examine evidence, consider alternatives, and defend your reasoning.
